terms.definition: An internal-alignment model checking seven interdependent elements — strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff, and skills — split into three 'hard' elements management can redraw on paper and four 'soft' ones that change only through behavior; a change fails when the seven fall out of alignment.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about why a reorganization stalled are scored on diagnosing a soft-element mismatch rather than proposing another org-chart redraw.

terms.definition: The emotional and rational reasons a customer makes a purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding motives helps position products around what matters.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Sets price to earn a stated percentage on invested capital: unit cost + (desired return x invested capital) / expected unit sales. Cost-plus pricing adds a flat markup no matter what the business has invested, so two firms with identical costs but very different capital bases price the same under cost-plus and differently under this method.
terms.whyItMatters: A manufacturer roleplay that names a required 20% return on a $2 million plant is asking for this calculation, and a markup answer will not satisfy the judge.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: An INTERNAL request from a department asking purchasing to buy something, carrying no commitment to any outside party; the purchase order that purchasing then issues is the EXTERNAL document, and it is the offer that forms a binding contract when the supplier accepts it.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing-control questions ask which document a department head signs and which one legally obligates the company; treating the internal request as the order is the standard error.

terms.definition: Total quota handed out across the sales force divided by the revenue the company actually forecasts. Assigning 1.1 to 1.3 times the target is deliberate over-assignment that absorbs ramping reps, mid-year attrition and under-performers, so the plan still lands if some reps miss — it measures quota against target, where pipeline coverage measures open deals against quota.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay that asks you to set quotas for next year is scored on whether you over-assign on purpose and can say why; the exam pairs this with pipeline coverage to see if you can tell the two ratios apart.

terms.definition: Vests copyright in the employer or commissioning party at the moment of creation instead of in the person who made the work, and it arises exactly two ways: a work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a specially commissioned work that falls into one of nine statutory categories and is covered by a signed written agreement. Anything else a freelancer creates stays theirs until assigned in writing.
terms.whyItMatters: A startup roleplay about who owns the logo a contract designer drew is decided by whether a signed assignment ever existed.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: A supplier-provided document in a fixed sixteen-section order under the Globally Harmonized System, covering hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and disposal — the fixed section order is the point, because a responder finds first-aid information in the same place on every sheet.
terms.whyItMatters: A chemical-spill roleplay expects you to say where the handling and first-aid instructions live and that the sheets must be accessible to employees on the shift, not filed in a manager's office.

terms.definition: Closed-won revenue divided by the number of deals won — $480,000 across 60 wins is $8,000 each. It measures one whole customer agreement, where average order value measures one transaction, so a customer who reorders four times a year raises order count without raising this figure at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking you to justify spending more selling time per account is answered by comparing deal size against cost per sales call, not by citing total revenue.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: Bandura's task-specific confidence that you can carry out a particular action, built from four sources in descending order of power — a personal mastery experience, watching a similar person succeed, verbal persuasion, and how one reads one's own physical arousal. Self-esteem, by contrast, is a global judgment of personal worth, so a person can hold high esteem and low efficacy on one specific task.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking how a manager raises a nervous employee's confidence for a first presentation wants a staged small success rather than a pep talk, since mastery outranks persuasion.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: The bureau's file of a consumer's accounts, balances and payment history — the underlying record, not the three-digit number calculated from it.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing a score in a roleplay has to correct the report first, since the score is only a summary of what the report says.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: An arrangement where the supplier monitors the buyer's usage data and decides replenishment timing and quantity, while the buyer still owns and pays for the stock on hand — consignment differs precisely there: the supplier retains ownership until the item is sold or consumed.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays ask who should hold the replenishment decision and who carries the cash tied up in the stock; the ownership line is what separates the two arrangements.

terms.definition: Every open deal multiplied by the win probability its current stage carries, then summed. A $200,000 deal sitting in a 30 percent stage counts as $60,000, so $1.4 million of raw pipeline spread across early stages may weight to under $400,000 — the total becomes a forecast instead of a list of what is theoretically in play.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting items give a table of deal values and stage probabilities and expect the weighted total, not the sum; in a roleplay defending a forecast to a manager, quoting raw pipeline reads as the rookie answer.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: Analyzing the current workforce and forecasting future talent needs.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures a business has the right people and skills to meet its goals.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: Splits a revenue miss into three computed pieces that must add back to the total gap: price variance = (actual price − planned price) × actual units; volume variance = (actual units − planned units) × planned price; mix variance = the shift in each product's share of total units valued at planned prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review items give planned and actual price, units and product split and expect all three figures; answering that sales came in soft without the decomposition is exactly what the rubric withholds credit for.

terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: A route into a second state's professional licence that accepts a licence already held in good standing elsewhere — for CPAs, commonly practice in four of the last ten years plus education and exam requirements the receiving board judges substantially equivalent — instead of requiring the applicant to sit that state's own examination again. It runs one direction only, which is what separates it from reciprocity: the receiving state grants the privilege and the sending state owes nothing in return.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay in which the judge plays an accountant relocating for a promotion turns on whether they must re-test, and exam items on advancement patterns expect this route named rather than a vague 'get licensed again.'

terms.definition: Recordable injuries and illnesses multiplied by 200,000, divided by total hours worked — the 200,000 representing 100 full-time employees working a 2,000-hour year, which is what makes a small firm's figure comparable with a large one's.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety roleplays give an injury count and an hours-worked total and ask whether the site is above its industry benchmark; a raw injury count cannot be benchmarked and is scored as an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Purchase price plus installation, training, consumables, maintenance and downtime across the asset's life, minus its resale value — so a $12,000 machine burning $400 of supplies a year beats a $9,000 machine burning $1,600 within five years. It answers a price objection by moving the comparison from acquisition price to lifetime cost.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer says a competitor quoted less, judges look for this calculation rather than a discount, because conceding on price is the response the rubric marks down.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.definition: Porter's decomposition of a firm into five primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and four support activities (procurement, technology development, human resource management, firm infrastructure), pricing the margin each one adds so low-value links can be outsourced.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where a manufacturer should cut cost without hurting the customer is answered by naming the specific link in the chain and the margin it contributes.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Isolates the profit effect of selling a different blend than planned: for each item, (its actual share of total units − its planned share) × total actual units × that item's planned contribution per unit, summed across the line — so a firm can hit its unit target exactly and still miss profit by shifting volume onto the thinner-margin product.
terms.whyItMatters: Shortfall questions where total units met plan are solved with this term alone, and it is the numeric case for paying sales incentives on contribution rather than on units sold.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: Splits the charge into a fixed access fee plus a per-unit price - a club's annual dues plus a per-round greens fee. Because the entry fee captures buyer surplus up front, the usage charge can sit near variable cost, which a single straight per-unit price could never do without giving up the fixed-fee revenue entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Membership and subscription roleplays ask how to raise revenue without raising the usage price, and splitting the charge in two is the move a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Ramped headcount times individual quota times the attainment rate the team really achieves — 20 reps carrying $500,000 each but hitting 70 percent supports $7 million of revenue, not the $10 million the quota sheet implies. Skipping the attainment factor is what makes a hiring plan promise revenue the team has never once delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: A growth-planning roleplay that asks how many reps to hire to reach a revenue goal is graded on multiplying in historical attainment; the exam tests it as a three-factor calculation.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Protection lasting indefinitely, but only while three conditions hold: the information draws independent economic value from not being generally known, it is not readily ascertainable by proper means, and the owner takes reasonable measures to keep it secret through NDAs, access limits and labeling. The Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 added a federal civil claim for misappropriation. The trade-off against a patent is disclosure — a patent publishes the invention for about twenty years of exclusivity, while lawful reverse engineering destroys a secret with no remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: IP roleplays comparing a beverage recipe to a bottling machine ask which protection fits, and reverse-engineering risk is the deciding fact.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: The average signed error across periods — actual minus forecast with the plus and minus signs kept — so persistent over-forecasting shows up as a running negative. It measures direction, where MAPE measures size, and a plan can post a respectable MAPE while drifting the same way every single month.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-review items give a run of months that miss high every time and ask what is wrong with the method; the answer is a systematic error in the assumptions, not random noise.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: How many times inventory is sold and replaced over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Turnover reveals inventory efficiency and its impact on cash flow.

terms.definition: Diagnosing the buyer's problem through questioning and recommending the right fit even when that means a smaller order, as against transactional selling, which moves a known item at speed and treats the exchange as complete at the register. The dividing line is who defines the need: the buyer arrives with it in a transaction, the rep uncovers it here.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer asks for a product that will not solve their stated problem, the rubric credits the competitor who redirects the recommendation over the one who rings up the request.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Rogers' model dividing adopters over time into five fixed bands measured in standard deviations from the mean adoption date — innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34% and laggards 16% — so the opinion-leading early adopters are a narrow 13.5% band that must be won before the 34% early majority will move, and a launch plan aimed at the mass market from day one is aimed at people who are not yet buying.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target first; naming the band and its percentage is what turns 'we'll target trendsetters' into a defensible answer.

terms.term: French and Raven's five bases of power
terms.definition: Distinguishes five sources of influence — legitimate power from the position, reward power, coercive power, expert power from demonstrated knowledge, and referent power from personal respect — with the first three attached to the role and the last two to the individual. Expert and referent power produce commitment; coercive power produces compliance only while someone is watching.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a new team lead with no formal authority to get cooperation is scored on building expert and referent power, and exam items on using power appropriately turn on that split.

terms.definition: The percentage change in unit sales delivered by a one-percent change in advertising spending — 3% more volume on 10% more spend is 0.3 — and because measured values usually sit near 0.1 to 0.2, doubling the budget rarely comes close to doubling volume; compare it against price elasticity before choosing which lever to pull.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget-allocation items supply both elasticities and expect the higher-return lever chosen with the arithmetic shown; a plan that asks for more advertising without this number has no answer when the judge asks why not a price move instead.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: Inspecting products and services to ensure they meet set standards.
terms.whyItMatters: It catches defects early, protecting satisfaction and reducing waste.

terms.definition: Count of deals where the buyer bought nothing at all, divided by all closed-lost deals — not by all opportunities. If 60 of 100 losses were no-decisions, the problem is urgency and the business case, because a buyer who chose a rival was at least persuaded to purchase; splitting losses this way points at two completely different fixes.
terms.whyItMatters: A win-loss review roleplay is scored on separating the two loss types before recommending anything, and the exam plants a competitor-versus-status-quo distinction in the stem.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: A court order directing an employer to withhold part of a worker's pay and send it to a creditor, capped by federal law as a share of disposable earnings.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the end point of the debt-control storyline in a personal-finance roleplay, and it reaches the paycheck without the debtor's consent.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.

terms.definition: Carries advertising effect forward as this week's effect = this week's spending effect + (retention rate × last week's carried effect); at a retention rate of 0.7 a flight that ends today still delivers 70% of its pull next week and 49% the week after, which is why a brand can stop spending and not lose sales immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-scheduling questions ask whether a brand can go dark for a month, and this decay arithmetic answers it; it also fixes how long after a campaign ends a plan may still credit sales to that campaign.

terms.definition: Ownership of employer retirement contributions earned in slices — commonly 20% after two years of service and 20% each year thereafter, reaching 100% at six years, so an employee leaving at year four keeps 60%. The alternative, cliff vesting, gives 0% until a single date and 100% on it, capped by law at three years for defined contribution plans; employee deferrals are always 100% vested from the first dollar under either schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay what a departing employee takes with them, you must apply the schedule to the years of service instead of assuming the whole account balance.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: The square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order) divided by annual holding cost per unit — the single order size where rising carrying cost and falling ordering cost cross and total cost bottoms out.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that asks you to cut the cost of holding stock is answered with this trade-off, not with 'order less': you must say that ordering more often lowers carrying cost but raises order cost, and name the quantity where the two balance.
